title: Type System and Type Inference
description: How TypeScript infers types and why explicit annotations are not always necessary.

blocks.content: TypeScript is a statically checked layer on top of JavaScript. It analyzes your code before runtime and tries to infer types from values and usage. For example, `let age = 30` is inferred as `number`, so writing `age = 'thirty'` later is a compile-time error. Good TypeScript does not mean adding a type annotation everywhere; it means allowing inference where the type is obvious and adding explicit types at important boundaries such as public APIs, function contracts, shared models, and external data.
keyPoints: Type inference reduces unnecessary type annotations while keeping type safety.
`const` usually produces narrower types than `let` because the value cannot be reassigned.
Explicit return types are useful on public/shared functions because they make the contract clear and prevent accidental return-shape changes.

blocks.explanation: The compiler can infer the local variable and return types. The parameter types are explicit because JavaScript values alone do not tell TypeScript what callers are allowed to pass.

blocks.question: Should you explicitly type every variable in a large TypeScript application?
blocks.answer: No. Prefer inference for obvious local values and add explicit types where they improve the contract: function parameters, public APIs, reusable models, component/service boundaries, and values coming from external systems.
blocks.explanation: Over-annotating creates noise and can even widen useful literal types. The goal is a strong type contract, not the maximum number of annotations.

title: Primitive and Literal Types
description: Using primitive, literal, and literal-union types to express valid values precisely.

blocks.content: TypeScript supports JavaScript primitive types such as `string`, `number`, `boolean`, `bigint`, `symbol`, `null`, and `undefined`. It can also represent an exact value as a literal type. A field like `status: 'idle' | 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'` is much safer than `status: string` because the compiler rejects unsupported status values.
keyPoints: Prefer lowercase primitive types like `string` and `number`, not wrapper types such as `String` and `Number`.
Literal unions are excellent for finite states such as status, role, theme, and difficulty.
Literal types improve autocomplete and eliminate many invalid runtime states.

blocks.explanation: The literal union describes the complete set of values accepted by the domain instead of allowing any arbitrary string.

blocks.question: What is the practical difference between `string` and the literal type `'admin'`?
blocks.answer: `string` accepts every string value. `'admin'` accepts exactly one string value: `admin`.
blocks.explanation: Literal types make domain rules visible to the compiler and are the building blocks for discriminated unions.

title: Arrays, Tuples and Readonly Tuples
description: Typing homogeneous collections and fixed-position data safely.

blocks.content: An array represents a collection of values of the same element type, such as `Topic[]` or `Array<Topic>`. A tuple represents a fixed sequence where each position has a known type, such as `[string, number]`. Tuples are useful when position has meaning, but for complex business data an object is usually clearer. `readonly` arrays and tuples prevent accidental mutation through that reference.
keyPoints: `T[]` and `Array<T>` are equivalent for normal arrays.
Tuples can define optional and rest elements.
`readonly T[]` prevents methods like `push`, `pop`, and assignment through an index.

blocks.explanation: Named tuple elements make positional values easier to understand, while the readonly array protects the collection from mutation through `topicIds`.

blocks.question: Would you model a user as `[string, string, number, boolean]` or as an interface with named properties?
blocks.answer: Use an interface/object for business entities. A tuple is better for small fixed-position values where the positions are naturally meaningful, such as a coordinate pair or a function returning two closely related values.
blocks.explanation: Long tuples become difficult to read and easy to misuse because callers must remember what every index means.

title: null, undefined and Optional Properties
description: Modeling absent values accurately with strict null checking.

blocks.content: With strict null checking enabled, `null` and `undefined` are not automatically assignable to every type. An optional property like `middleName?: string` means the property may be absent and reading it produces `string | undefined`. A property written as `middleName: string | null` must exist but may intentionally contain `null`. That distinction matters when modeling API contracts.
keyPoints: `prop?: T` means the property may be missing.
`prop: T | null` means the property is required but null is a valid value.
Use optional chaining (`?.`) and nullish coalescing (`??`) to handle missing values clearly.

blocks.explanation: The model differentiates an omitted avatar from a last-login field whose business value can explicitly be null.

blocks.question: Why is `strictNullChecks` important in production applications?
blocks.answer: It forces the compiler to make absence explicit. That catches many 'cannot read properties of undefined/null' bugs before runtime and makes API models more truthful.
blocks.explanation: Without strict null checking, nullable values can flow into places that assume a real value exists.

title: Function Types and Callbacks
description: Typing parameters, return values, callbacks, optional parameters, and rest parameters.

blocks.content: TypeScript can describe a function itself as a type. This is especially useful for callbacks, event handlers, strategies, and higher-order functions. Function parameters can be required, optional, have defaults, or collect remaining arguments with rest syntax. A return type of `void` means callers should not depend on a returned value; it does not mean the implementation is physically incapable of returning one.
keyPoints: Function types make callback contracts explicit.
Optional parameters must normally follow required parameters.
Use `(...args: T[])` for a variable number of arguments of the same type.

blocks.explanation: The callback contract is reusable and consumers get type checking and autocomplete for its parameters.

blocks.question: You pass callbacks through several services and components, but each place writes `(data: any) => any`. What is the main TypeScript problem?
blocks.answer: The callback boundary has effectively opted out of type safety. Define a reusable function type or generic callback so input and output relationships remain checked.
blocks.explanation: Strong callback types prevent incorrect argument shapes and make refactoring much safer.

title: Function Overloads
description: Providing multiple call signatures for one implementation.

blocks.content: Function overloads let one implementation expose multiple strongly typed ways to call it. You write one or more overload signatures followed by a single implementation signature that is compatible with all overloads. Callers see the overload signatures, not the broad implementation signature.
keyPoints: Overloads are useful when the return type depends on the input shape.
The implementation signature must handle every declared overload.
If a union parameter expresses the API clearly, prefer the simpler union over unnecessary overloads.

blocks.explanation: Each overload gives callers a precise return type even though one implementation handles both cases.

blocks.question: When would you prefer overloads instead of a single union-typed parameter?
blocks.answer: Use overloads when different input forms produce meaningfully different output types or accepted parameter combinations. Use a union when the input differs but the output contract is essentially the same.
blocks.explanation: Overloads should improve caller precision, not just make the declaration longer.

blocks.title: The overload you cannot call
blocks.question: A function exposes overloads for string and number, with an implementation accepting string | number. Why can a caller holding string | number still fail overload resolution?
blocks.answer: Calls are checked against the public overload signatures, not the implementation signature. Neither individual overload necessarily accepts the caller's union.
blocks.explanation:
Add an appropriate union overload or use a union parameter when separate overloads do not express a useful input/output relationship.

[Further reading](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/functions.html)
hints: Which signatures are visible to callers?

title: Type Narrowing and Type Guards
description: Safely reducing a broad type to a more specific type based on runtime checks.

blocks.content: Narrowing is TypeScript's control-flow analysis that starts with a broad type and makes it more specific after a runtime check. Common guards include `typeof`, `instanceof`, the `in` operator, equality checks, truthiness checks, and discriminant properties. Narrowing is preferable to blindly asserting a type because the runtime condition actually proves something about the value.
keyPoints: `typeof` is appropriate for primitives.
`instanceof` works with real runtime classes/constructors.
`in` narrows object unions based on property existence.
TypeScript tracks narrowing through control flow and often restores the broader type outside the guarded branch.

blocks.explanation: Inside the first branch `id` is a number; after that branch returns, TypeScript knows the remaining path must contain a string.

blocks.question: Why is `value as User` not equivalent to checking that `value` is actually a User?
blocks.answer: A type assertion only tells the compiler to trust you; it creates no runtime validation. A type guard performs a real check and lets the compiler narrow based on evidence.
blocks.explanation: Assertions can hide invalid external data and move the failure from compile time to runtime.

title: Custom Type Predicates and Assertion Functions
description: Creating reusable runtime validation functions that also narrow types for the compiler.

blocks.content: A custom type predicate has a return type such as `value is User`. If the function returns true, TypeScript narrows the value to `User` in that branch. An assertion function such as `asserts value is User` can throw when validation fails; after it returns successfully, TypeScript treats the value as `User`. These are useful at external-data boundaries.
keyPoints: A type predicate returns boolean and narrows in a conditional branch.
An assertion function normally throws on invalid input and narrows after the call.
The annotation does not magically validate data; the implementation must perform correct runtime checks.

blocks.explanation: The runtime guard and compile-time narrowing are connected through the `value is User` return type.

blocks.question: Your application imports a JSON backup file created by a user. Should you cast the parsed value directly to your application model?
blocks.answer: No. Treat the parsed data as `unknown`, validate the required structure at runtime, and then narrow it with a type predicate or schema validator.
blocks.explanation: TypeScript types disappear at runtime, so external input always needs runtime validation.

blocks.title: A type guard that lies
blocks.question: Can a function declared `isUser(x: unknown): x is User` simply return true and convince the compiler?
blocks.answer: Yes. An explicit predicate is a contract supplied by its author; the compiler does not prove that its implementation validates every User field.
blocks.explanation:
A faulty predicate makes later code look safe while accepting invalid values. Implement actual checks and test malformed inputs, missing fields, and nested structures.

[Further reading](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html)
hints: Who is responsible for the predicate's truth?

title: never and Exhaustiveness Checking
description: Understanding impossible values and using never to catch unhandled cases.

blocks.content: `never` represents a value that should never occur. A function that always throws can return `never`, and a variable can narrow to `never` after all possible union members have been handled. This makes `never` especially useful for exhaustive `switch` checks.
keyPoints: `never` is different from `void`: `void` represents an ignored/absent useful return value, while `never` means execution cannot produce a value.
An exhaustive guard fails to compile when a union gains a new unhandled member.
Impossible intersections can also reduce to `never`.

blocks.explanation: If `Status` later adds `'error'`, the default branch no longer receives `never`, so the compiler points out the missing case.

blocks.question: What is the practical value of the `const impossible: never = value` pattern?
blocks.answer: It converts an unhandled union member into a compile-time error, forcing code to be updated when the union changes.
blocks.explanation: This is a low-cost way to protect state machines, reducers, rendering logic, and business-status switches.

blocks.title: A default branch hides a missing case
blocks.question: You add a new discriminated-union variant, but an old switch still compiles because default returns an empty string. How can you detect the missing case?
blocks.answer: In the fallback, assign the remaining value to never or pass it to an assertNever function. An unhandled variant then causes a compile-time error.
blocks.explanation:
A default branch is not automatically an exhaustiveness check. Keep runtime fallback behavior separate from proof that all declared variants were handled.

[Further reading](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/narrowing.html)
hints: What type remains after every case is eliminated?

title: Type Assertions and Non-null Assertion
description: Using `as`, `!`, and assertions carefully without hiding real runtime problems.

blocks.content: A type assertion such as `value as User` tells the compiler that you know more than it can prove. The non-null assertion `value!` tells the compiler that `null` and `undefined` are impossible at that point. Neither operator performs a runtime check, so both should be used only when the guarantee comes from logic the compiler cannot see.
keyPoints: Assertions do not transform or validate runtime values.
Prefer narrowing, optional chaining, or explicit guards when possible.
Frequent `!` usage can be a sign that lifecycle or data-flow assumptions are not modeled clearly.

blocks.question: Does `const user = apiValue as User` convert `apiValue` into a User object?
blocks.answer: No. It changes only the compiler's view of the value. The JavaScript object at runtime is unchanged.
blocks.explanation: If the data is invalid, the assertion can make unsafe code compile without preventing a runtime failure.

blocks.question: A codebase uses `response.data!.user!.profile!.name` everywhere. What would you improve?
blocks.answer: Model the nullable states honestly and use guards, optional chaining, defaults, or earlier validation. Keep `!` only where the invariant is truly guaranteed.
blocks.explanation: Repeated non-null assertions usually hide uncertainty instead of resolving it.

title: Generic Constraints and keyof Generics
description: Restricting generic parameters while preserving precise relationships between values.

blocks.content: A generic constraint uses `extends` to say that a generic type must satisfy a minimum shape. This lets the implementation safely use known members without losing the caller's more specific type. A common pattern is `<T, K extends keyof T>` for functions that accept a valid property key and return `T[K]`.
keyPoints: Constraints limit what types are accepted but preserve the caller's exact subtype.
`K extends keyof T` prevents invalid property names.
The return type `T[K]` stays connected to the selected key.

blocks.explanation: The key is restricted to actual keys of the object, and the result type changes according to the selected key.

blocks.question: Why is `<T, K extends keyof T>` safer than `(obj: any, key: string): any`?
blocks.answer: It rejects invalid keys, preserves autocomplete, and returns the exact property type instead of losing all information to `any`.
blocks.explanation: This pattern is widely useful in reusable table, form, sorting, filtering, and configuration utilities.

title: Generic Interfaces and Classes
description: Applying generic type parameters to reusable data structures, contracts, and services.

blocks.content: Generics are not limited to functions. Interfaces and classes can expose type parameters so one reusable structure keeps strong typing for different data models. Examples include API responses, pagination, repositories, caches, form state, and event payloads.
keyPoints: A generic interface keeps the same structure while allowing the contained data type to vary.
Multiple generic parameters can describe relationships such as key/value or request/response.
Default generic parameters can reduce boilerplate for common cases.

blocks.explanation: The common response metadata is reused while the payload remains strongly typed as `Topic[]`.

blocks.question: Your application has `UserResponse`, `TopicResponse`, `ProjectResponse`, and `ReportResponse`, all with identical metadata and only a different `data` field. What would you change?
blocks.answer: Create one generic `ApiResponse<T>` and supply the payload type at each usage site.
blocks.explanation: This removes duplicate models while preserving precise payload types.

title: Indexed Access Types
description: Reading a property type from another type using bracket notation.

blocks.content: Indexed access types use syntax like `User['id']` to obtain the type of a property from an existing type. You can index with a union of keys or with `keyof` to derive larger unions. This helps keep related types synchronized instead of repeating primitive or union definitions manually.
keyPoints: `T[K]` means 'the type of property K on T'.
Indexing with a union of keys produces a union of the corresponding property types.
`typeof array[number]` is a common way to derive the element type of a readonly const array.

blocks.explanation: If the source property changes later, the derived type changes automatically.

blocks.question: Why derive `type Priority = Topic['priority']` instead of rewriting the literal union again?
blocks.answer: It creates one source of truth. The derived type cannot silently drift away from the model's actual property type.
blocks.explanation: Derived types make large codebases safer during refactoring.

title: Mapped Types
description: Transforming every property in an existing type using `keyof` and property mapping.

blocks.content: A mapped type iterates over a union of property keys and creates a new object type. Built-in utilities such as `Partial`, `Readonly`, and `Required` are based on this idea. Mapped types can add or remove `readonly` and optional modifiers and can remap keys with an `as` clause.
keyPoints: The core pattern is `[K in keyof T]: ...`.
Modifiers can be added or removed with `?`, `-?`, `readonly`, and `-readonly`.
Mapped types are compile-time transformations; they do not copy or change runtime objects.

blocks.explanation: The keys are copied from `Permissions`, while every property value type is transformed to boolean.

blocks.question: What TypeScript feature is behind utility types such as `Partial<T>` and `Readonly<T>`?
blocks.answer: Mapped types. They iterate over `keyof T` and change the modifiers or value type of each property.
blocks.explanation: Understanding mapped types makes advanced utility types much easier to read and create.

title: Conditional Types
description: Selecting one type or another based on a type relationship.

blocks.content: A conditional type has the form `T extends U ? X : Y`. It performs a compile-time type decision: if `T` is assignable to `U`, TypeScript produces `X`; otherwise it produces `Y`. Conditional types become especially powerful with generics and can distribute over union types.
keyPoints: Conditional types operate only at compile time.
When the checked type is a naked generic parameter, conditional types often distribute over unions.
Many built-in utility types use conditional types internally.

blocks.explanation: The first type maps dates to a serialized string type, while the second removes nullish members from a union through distribution.

blocks.question: What does `T extends U ? X : Y` mean in a type alias?
blocks.answer: It is a conditional type: if T is assignable to U, the result is X; otherwise the result is Y.
blocks.explanation: It is similar to a type-level if/else, but it does not execute at runtime.

blocks.title: A conditional type splits a union
blocks.question: What is `T extends string ? T[] : never` for T = string | number, and why is it not never?
blocks.answer: With a naked type parameter, the conditional distributes over the union. The result is string[]. Wrap both sides, such as [T] extends [string], when you want a check of the whole union.
blocks.explanation:
The whole union is not assignable to string, but distribution tests each member separately before combining the results.

[Further reading](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/conditional-types.html)
hints: Does the conditional examine one member or the entire union?

title: The infer Keyword
description: Extracting a type from another type inside conditional types.

blocks.content: `infer` introduces a temporary type variable inside the true branch pattern of a conditional type. It is commonly used to extract a function's return type, an array's element type, a promise's resolved value, or part of a tuple. You normally see it in reusable type utilities rather than day-to-day business models.
keyPoints: `infer` is available inside the `extends` pattern of a conditional type.
It extracts a type instead of requiring the caller to provide it separately.
Built-in helpers such as `ReturnType` are based on the same idea.

blocks.explanation: `U` captures the array element type and `R` captures a function's return type.

blocks.question: Is `infer` a runtime keyword that reads a JavaScript value?
blocks.answer: No. It exists only in TypeScript's type system and is erased completely from the emitted JavaScript.
blocks.explanation: Its purpose is extracting relationships between types at compile time.

title: Template Literal Types
description: Building precise string types from unions and string patterns.

blocks.content: Template literal types use JavaScript-like template string syntax in the type system to construct string literal unions. They are useful for event names, route keys, CSS-like property conventions, translation keys, action names, and strongly typed configuration identifiers.
keyPoints: Interpolating a union creates all resulting string combinations.
They work well with utility types such as `Uppercase`, `Lowercase`, `Capitalize`, and `Uncapitalize`.
Use them when a string follows a predictable domain pattern; avoid excessive complexity for arbitrary strings.

blocks.explanation: The compiler builds the valid event-name combinations instead of accepting any string.

blocks.question: Your event bus expects names like `user:created`, `user:deleted`, `topic:created`, and `topic:deleted`. How can TypeScript prevent typos without manually writing every string?
blocks.answer: Use literal unions for the entity and action, then combine them with a template literal type.
blocks.explanation: This keeps the allowed event-name pattern centralized and autocomplete-friendly.

title: as const and Literal Inference
description: Preserving literal values and readonly object/tuple shapes with const assertions.

blocks.content: `as const` tells TypeScript to infer the narrowest literal types for a literal expression and mark object properties/array elements readonly in that inferred type. It is useful for defining configuration constants from which you want to derive unions.
keyPoints: String values stay literal instead of widening to `string`.
Array literals become readonly tuples.
Object properties become readonly in the inferred type.
It is a compile-time assertion and does not freeze the JavaScript object at runtime.

blocks.explanation: The runtime constants become a source from which exact compile-time types can be derived.

blocks.question: What is the difference between declaring a variable with `const` and writing `as const`?
blocks.answer: `const` prevents reassignment of the variable binding. `as const` additionally asks TypeScript to infer literal/readonly types deeply across the literal expression's immediate structure.
blocks.explanation: A const object variable can still have writable properties unless its type makes them readonly.

title: The satisfies Operator
description: Validating that a value conforms to a type without unnecessarily replacing its inferred type.

blocks.content: The `satisfies` operator checks that an expression is assignable to a target type while preserving useful information from the expression's own inferred type. It is especially useful for configuration objects where you want validation of required keys and value shapes without unnecessarily widening everything to the declared interface.
keyPoints: `satisfies` performs a compatibility check but does not cast the value.
It often preserves more specific property information than a broad type annotation.
It is useful for maps, route/config objects, and lookup tables that must match a contract.

blocks.explanation: The object must contain the required keys and shapes, while TypeScript still keeps the expression's useful inferred structure.

blocks.question: Does `value satisfies SomeType` convert the value to `SomeType`?
blocks.answer: No. It checks compatibility at compile time while keeping the value's inferred type; it performs no runtime conversion.
blocks.explanation: This is why `satisfies` is often safer and more precise for configuration objects than an assertion.

title: Enums vs Literal Unions
description: Choosing between runtime enum objects and compile-time literal-union modeling.

blocks.content: Both enums and literal unions can represent a finite set of allowed values, but they have different runtime behavior. A normal TypeScript enum produces a runtime JavaScript value, while a union such as `'admin' | 'user'` exists only for type checking. Literal unions often integrate naturally with JSON and APIs because the values are already plain strings.
keyPoints: Use literal unions when you mainly need compile-time restriction of plain string/number values.
Use an enum when a runtime namespace/value object is genuinely useful and fits the project style.
Do not choose an enum simply because the domain has a finite list; consider serialization and runtime needs.

blocks.explanation: The union works naturally with the same string values an API or JSON payload would usually contain.

blocks.question: Why do many TypeScript codebases prefer string literal unions over enums for API status values?
blocks.answer: Literal unions have no generated runtime object, align directly with serialized string values, and work naturally with narrowing and discriminated unions.
blocks.explanation: Enums are still valid, but the decision should be based on runtime and modeling needs rather than habit.

title: Structural Typing and Type Compatibility
description: Why TypeScript compares compatible shapes rather than requiring explicit nominal relationships.

blocks.content: TypeScript uses structural typing for most object compatibility: if a value has at least the members required by a target type with compatible types, it can usually be assigned even if it never explicitly declared that interface. This matches JavaScript's flexible object model and is sometimes described as compile-time duck typing.
keyPoints: Type compatibility is mostly based on shape, not type names.
An object may have extra properties and still be assignable through an existing variable.
Fresh object literals receive additional excess-property checking to catch likely mistakes.

blocks.explanation: `Employee` does not need to explicitly implement `Named`; its public structure is already compatible.

blocks.question: Why can two unrelated interfaces sometimes accept the same object in TypeScript?
blocks.answer: Because TypeScript generally checks their structure. If the object's members satisfy the required shape, explicit inheritance or a shared nominal type name is not required.
blocks.explanation: This behavior is fundamental to understanding assignability in TypeScript.

title: Excess Property Checks
description: Understanding why fresh object literals are checked more strictly for unexpected properties.

blocks.content: Although TypeScript is structurally typed, fresh object literals get an additional excess-property check when assigned to a known object type. This is meant to catch typos or accidental fields. Once the same value exists in a variable, normal structural compatibility rules may allow extra properties as long as the required ones are present.
keyPoints: Fresh object literals are checked more strictly for unknown keys.
The rule helps detect likely mistakes such as misspelled configuration properties.
Do not bypass the check with assertions unless the extra property is genuinely intentional and the target API can handle it.

blocks.question: Why can these two assignments behave differently?
blocks.answer: The first value is a fresh object literal and receives excess-property checking. The second assignment checks whether `temp` has at least the required compatible members of `User`.
blocks.explanation: This is an intentional TypeScript usability rule layered on top of structural typing.

blocks.question: Should you add `[key: string]: any` to an interface just to silence excess-property errors?
blocks.answer: Usually no. That weakens the contract dramatically. First determine whether extra keys are actually part of the domain and, if so, model them with a meaningful index signature or `Record` value type.
blocks.explanation: A broad any index signature can hide misspellings and incompatible data.

blocks.title: A variable bypasses the excess-property check
blocks.question: Why can passing a variable with extra fields succeed when passing the same object literal directly to a function produces an excess-property error?
blocks.answer: Fresh object literals receive an extra excess-property check. Normal structural assignability can allow a variable with the required fields and additional fields.
blocks.explanation:
This does not make runtime objects exact or strip their extra keys. Validate or select fields explicitly at a trust boundary.

[Further reading](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/objects.html)

title: Index Signatures and Record
description: Typing dictionary-like objects whose keys are not all known individually.

blocks.content: An index signature describes the type of properties whose exact names are not known in advance, such as `{ [key: string]: TopicProgress }`. `Record<K, V>` is a utility type for building a dictionary with key type `K` and value type `V`. When the set of keys is known as a literal union, `Record` is especially useful because it can require every key.
keyPoints: Use an index signature for genuinely open-ended keys.
Use `Record<'a' | 'b', V>` when a finite key set should be complete.
Avoid `Record<string, any>` when a meaningful value type can be defined.

blocks.explanation: Every difficulty key is required, so forgetting one becomes a compile-time error.

blocks.question: When is `Record<K, V>` better than `{ [key: string]: V }`?
blocks.answer: When the valid keys can be represented by a specific union. `Record` can then enforce that those keys exist and prevent unrelated keys.
blocks.explanation: A broad string index signature is appropriate only when keys are truly dynamic.

blocks.title: Record does not create keys
blocks.question: Does `const users: Record<string, User> = {}` guarantee that `users['missing']` is a User at runtime?
blocks.answer: No. Record describes a type; it does not populate the object. Enable noUncheckedIndexedAccess for safer unchecked indexing, or model possibly missing values explicitly.
blocks.explanation:
Handle absent entries before using them. Compile-time index signatures can otherwise promise more than the data structure actually contains.

[Further reading](https://www.typescriptlang.org/tsconfig/noUncheckedIndexedAccess.html)
hints: What value does an absent JavaScript property return?

title: readonly and Immutability
description: Using readonly properties and collections to prevent accidental mutation at compile time.

blocks.content: `readonly` prevents assignment to a property through a given TypeScript reference. `Readonly<T>` applies this to all top-level properties and `readonly T[]` prevents collection mutation methods. This is compile-time protection; it does not automatically deep-freeze the runtime object.
keyPoints: `readonly` communicates ownership and mutation expectations.
`Readonly<T>` is shallow, not deep.
Readonly models work well with immutable state-update patterns.

blocks.explanation: Only the identity field is readonly; the title remains intentionally editable.

blocks.question: Does `Readonly<User>` make nested objects deeply immutable?
blocks.answer: No. The built-in `Readonly<T>` only makes the top-level properties readonly. Nested objects need their own readonly types or a recursive utility.
blocks.explanation: This distinction matters when designing immutable state structures.

title: Classes and Access Modifiers
description: Using public, private, protected, readonly, parameter properties, and class contracts.

blocks.content: TypeScript extends JavaScript classes with compile-time access modifiers such as `public`, `private`, and `protected`, plus `readonly` fields and parameter-property shorthand. `public` is the default. `private` restricts access to the declaring class in TypeScript, while `protected` also allows subclasses. These modifiers help express encapsulation but you should still understand the runtime JavaScript that is emitted.
keyPoints: `public` members are accessible anywhere.
`private` members are accessible only inside the declaring class.
`protected` members are available inside the class and subclasses.
Constructor parameter properties can declare and initialize fields in one step.

blocks.explanation: The constructor shorthand creates a private readonly `apiUrl` property and initializes it from the constructor argument.

blocks.question: What is the difference between `private` and `protected`?
blocks.answer: `private` is accessible only within the declaring class; `protected` is also accessible within subclasses.
blocks.explanation: Use the narrowest visibility that still supports the intended design.

title: Abstract Classes, extends and implements
description: Understanding inheritance and contract implementation in TypeScript.

blocks.content: `extends` inherits implementation and instance behavior from another class. `implements` checks that a class satisfies an interface/type contract but does not copy implementation. An abstract class can provide shared implementation while requiring subclasses to implement abstract members, and it cannot be instantiated directly.
keyPoints: `implements` is a compile-time conformance check.
`extends` creates a JavaScript inheritance relationship.
Abstract classes can contain both implemented and abstract members.
Prefer composition when inheritance does not represent a genuine 'is-a' relationship.

blocks.explanation: The abstract base shares behavior, while the interface describes the public contract.

blocks.question: Does `implements SomeInterface` add the interface's members to the class at runtime?
blocks.answer: No. Interfaces are erased from the emitted JavaScript. `implements` only asks the TypeScript compiler to verify that the class provides the required shape.
blocks.explanation: Runtime inheritance comes from `extends`, not from `implements`.

title: Modules, import and export
description: Organizing TypeScript code with ES modules and type-only imports.

blocks.content: A file with a top-level `import` or `export` is treated as a module. ES module syntax lets code expose public values and types while keeping other declarations file-scoped. TypeScript also supports `import type` and `export type` for dependencies that exist only in the type system.
keyPoints: Named exports make dependencies explicit and easy to refactor.
`import type` communicates that a dependency is used only for type checking.
Module resolution is controlled by compiler/tooling configuration and should match the target runtime or bundler.

blocks.explanation: `Topic` is needed only during type checking, so a type-only import makes that intent clear.

blocks.question: What is the benefit of `import type { User } from './user'`?
blocks.answer: It explicitly marks the import as type-only, helping the compiler/toolchain avoid treating it as a runtime dependency and making the code's intent clearer.
blocks.explanation: This becomes valuable when working with strict module settings and preventing accidental runtime import cycles.

title: Declaration Files and Module Augmentation
description: Understanding `.d.ts` files, ambient declarations, and safe augmentation of existing types.

blocks.content: Declaration files (`.d.ts`) describe types for JavaScript code or ambient APIs without providing runtime implementation. They are how TypeScript understands many JavaScript libraries and global browser/runtime values. Module augmentation lets you extend an existing module's declared interfaces when a library intentionally supports extension.
keyPoints: A `.d.ts` file describes runtime code that exists elsewhere.
`declare` tells TypeScript about a value without emitting an implementation.
Module/global augmentation should be narrow and intentional because it changes types across the program.

blocks.explanation: The declaration teaches TypeScript about a global runtime property without creating that property itself.

blocks.question: If you add a property to `Window` in a `.d.ts` file, does the browser automatically create that property at runtime?
blocks.answer: No. The declaration only informs TypeScript. Some script or runtime code must actually create the property.
blocks.explanation: Declaration files describe runtime reality; they do not produce it.

title: tsconfig and Strict Type Checking
description: Understanding compiler configuration and why strict mode matters in production code.

blocks.content: `tsconfig.json` controls how TypeScript interprets, checks, and emits a project. The `strict` option enables a family of stronger checks that catch unsafe assumptions around nullability, implicit `any`, function compatibility, class initialization, and more. Framework tooling may add or override related options, so developers should understand the effective configuration rather than copying flags blindly.
keyPoints: `strict: true` enables a set of important type-safety checks.
`noImplicitAny` prevents untyped parameters/values from silently becoming `any` in many cases.
`strictNullChecks` makes `null` and `undefined` explicit.
`noUncheckedIndexedAccess` can make indexed reads safer by including `undefined` when a key may be absent.

blocks.question: Why would a team enable strict mode even if it creates more compile errors during migration?
blocks.answer: Because the errors expose real uncertainty and unsafe assumptions that would otherwise remain hidden. The short-term migration work usually buys stronger refactoring confidence and fewer runtime failures.
blocks.explanation: Strictness is most valuable at boundaries where data can be absent or incorrectly shaped.

blocks.question: A legacy project has hundreds of implicit-any errors. Would you solve them by changing every affected type to `any`?
blocks.answer: No. Prioritize important boundaries, introduce real domain types, use `unknown` for uncertain external data, and migrate incrementally. Replacing errors with `any` keeps the same risk while hiding it from the compiler.
blocks.explanation: The purpose of strict migration is to increase information, not suppress diagnostics.

title: Promise and Async Function Typing
description: Typing asynchronous functions, Promise results, errors, and resolved values.

blocks.content: An `async` function always returns a Promise. If the logical result is `Topic[]`, the function's return type is `Promise<Topic[]>`. `await` unwraps the fulfilled value for normal control flow. TypeScript can type the fulfilled value, but rejected promises/errors still require runtime handling and should not be assumed to have a specific error shape.
keyPoints: `async function f(): Promise<T>` resolves to T.
`Awaited<T>` can derive the recursively awaited value type of a promise-like type.
Use `unknown` for caught errors when the project/compiler setting does not already enforce that behavior.

blocks.explanation: The return type models the asynchronous contract, and `Awaited<ReturnType<...>>` derives the fulfilled data type.

blocks.question: Can an `async function getCount(): number` be valid if it returns `5`?
blocks.answer: No. An async function returns a Promise, so its annotation must be `Promise<number>` even when the implementation writes `return 5`.
blocks.explanation: JavaScript automatically wraps the returned value in a resolved Promise.

title: Type-safe Error Handling
description: Handling catch values and external errors without assuming a shape that is not guaranteed.

blocks.content: JavaScript allows any value to be thrown, not only `Error` objects. Therefore safe TypeScript code should narrow a caught value before reading `.message` or custom fields. Treating an unknown error as `any` can cause a second error while handling the first one.
keyPoints: Use `error instanceof Error` before accessing standard Error members.
External libraries may throw custom values, so adapt or normalize them at a boundary.
A central error-normalization helper can simplify application-level handling.

blocks.explanation: The helper narrows several possible error shapes instead of assuming every thrown value has a `message` property.

blocks.question: Why is `catch (error: any)` unsafe?
blocks.answer: Because JavaScript can throw any value and `any` lets you access arbitrary fields without proof. `unknown` forces the handler to narrow or normalize the error first.
blocks.explanation: Error handling is exactly where false assumptions are common, so type safety is valuable.

title: Typing API and External Data Boundaries
description: Understanding why TypeScript types alone cannot guarantee server, storage, or user-provided data.

blocks.content: TypeScript checks your source code but its types are erased at runtime. An HTTP response, localStorage value, postMessage payload, uploaded JSON file, or third-party library can still contain invalid data. The safe boundary pattern is: receive an uncertain value, represent it as `unknown`, validate or parse it at runtime, and only then expose a trusted domain type to the rest of the application.
keyPoints: An interface does not validate an HTTP response.
Avoid casting external JSON directly to a trusted domain type.
Keep validation at boundaries so most application code can work with already-trusted types.
Schema-validation libraries can complement TypeScript when runtime validation is substantial.

blocks.explanation: Only validated data escapes the parsing function as a trusted `TopicSummary`.

blocks.question: An API is typed as `http.get<User>('/user')`. Does the generic type guarantee that the server really returned a valid User at runtime?
blocks.answer: No. It tells TypeScript what the application expects, but it does not validate the bytes coming from the server. Runtime validation is required when the boundary is not fully trusted.
blocks.explanation: This distinction is one of the most important production TypeScript concepts.

title: Optional Chaining and Nullish Coalescing
description: Safely reading optional values and choosing defaults without incorrectly treating valid falsy values as missing.

blocks.content: Optional chaining (`?.`) stops property access or a call when the value to its left is `null` or `undefined`. Nullish coalescing (`??`) uses a fallback only when the left side is `null` or `undefined`. This is different from `||`, which also treats values such as `0`, `false`, and an empty string as falsy.
keyPoints: `user.profile?.name` returns undefined instead of throwing when profile is nullish.
`count ?? 0` preserves a valid count of 0.
Use `||` when you genuinely mean any falsy value should fall back.

blocks.question: What are the values of `a` and `b`?
blocks.answer: `a` is 10 because 0 is falsy. `b` is 0 because nullish coalescing falls back only for null or undefined.
blocks.explanation: This difference frequently matters for valid numeric zeroes, empty text, and boolean false values.

blocks.question: When should you prefer `??` over `||`?
blocks.answer: When only `null` and `undefined` mean 'missing' and other falsy values are valid domain values.
blocks.explanation: It prevents legitimate values such as 0 or false from being replaced accidentally.

blocks.title: A valid zero replaced by a default
blocks.question: For `count = 0`, how do `count || 10` and `count ?? 10` differ?
blocks.answer: The first returns 10 because zero is falsy. The second returns 0 because nullish coalescing replaces only null or undefined.
blocks.explanation:
Use the operator that matches the domain. Empty strings, false, and zero are often legitimate user values.

[Further reading](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/release-notes/typescript-3-7.html)
hints: List which values each operator treats as absent.

title: Destructuring, Rest and Spread Typing
description: How TypeScript infers object/array destructuring and rest/spread operations.

blocks.content: TypeScript understands JavaScript destructuring, rest, and spread syntax and infers types from the source object or array. Destructured function parameters can be annotated with an object type. Spread is often used to create updated immutable objects, but developers should remember it is a shallow operation at runtime.
keyPoints: Annotate the whole destructured parameter shape rather than trying to type each variable separately.
Object spread creates a shallow copy.
Rest parameters and tuple types can precisely model variadic function arguments.

blocks.explanation: The function accepts only the fields it needs, and the spread expression creates a new object with `completed` changed.

blocks.question: Does `{ ...original }` create a deep copy that makes nested objects independent?
blocks.answer: No. Object spread is shallow; nested object references are still shared unless they are copied separately.
blocks.explanation: TypeScript does not change JavaScript's runtime copy semantics.

title: Variance and Function Type Compatibility
description: Understanding why callback parameter and return type compatibility can be subtle.

blocks.content: Variance describes how a type relationship behaves when a generic or function type contains another type. In function types, safe parameter compatibility works differently from return-value compatibility: a callback that requires a narrower parameter can be unsafe when the caller may provide a broader value. TypeScript's strict function checking catches many of these cases.
keyPoints: Function return values are generally safe to become more specific when assignment expectations allow it.
Function parameters require careful compatibility because the eventual caller controls the argument.
These rules explain many callback assignment errors that initially appear counter-intuitive.

blocks.explanation: A function that only knows how to handle Dogs cannot safely stand in for a function that promises to handle every Animal.

blocks.question: Why might assigning `(dog: Dog) => void` to `(animal: Animal) => void` be unsafe?
blocks.answer: Because the broader function type promises callers they may pass any Animal. The Dog-only implementation could then receive an Animal that has no Dog-specific members.
blocks.explanation: The assignment would break the contract expected by callers.

title: Branded Types for Domain IDs
description: Creating nominal-like distinctions between values that share the same primitive representation.

blocks.content: Because TypeScript is structurally typed, different IDs represented as plain strings are normally interchangeable. A branded type adds a compile-time marker so values such as `UserId` and `TopicId` cannot be accidentally mixed even though both are strings at runtime. This pattern is useful for high-value domain boundaries but should not be overused.
keyPoints: Brands provide nominal-like safety on top of structural typing.
The brand exists only in the type system; the runtime value can remain a plain string.
Create branded values through validated factories/parsers when possible.

blocks.explanation: The two IDs remain strings at runtime but are intentionally incompatible at compile time.

blocks.question: What problem do branded types solve in a structurally typed language?
blocks.answer: They distinguish domain values that have the same underlying shape, such as different kinds of string IDs, so they cannot be accidentally interchanged.
blocks.explanation: They add selected nominal-style constraints without changing the runtime representation.

title: Typing this in Functions and Classes
description: Understanding contextual `this`, explicit this parameters, and common callback pitfalls.

blocks.content: JavaScript's `this` is determined by how a normal function is called, while arrow functions capture `this` lexically. TypeScript can infer `this` in many methods and also supports a special fake first parameter such as `function f(this: HTMLElement, event: Event)` to describe the required call context. Understanding runtime `this` behavior is still necessary; TypeScript only checks it.
keyPoints: Arrow functions do not create their own `this` binding.
Passing an unbound class method as a callback can lose its expected runtime `this`.
Explicit `this` parameters are erased from emitted JavaScript and exist only for checking.

blocks.question: A class method works when called as `service.load()` but fails after being passed directly as a callback. Why?
blocks.answer: The call site may no longer provide the class instance as `this`. Bind the method, wrap it in an arrow callback, or design the method as an arrow-property callback when that tradeoff is appropriate.
blocks.explanation: This is a JavaScript runtime behavior that TypeScript can help describe but cannot automatically fix.

blocks.question: Does an explicit TypeScript `this` parameter become a real JavaScript argument?
blocks.answer: No. It is a compile-time-only parameter used for checking the expected call context.
blocks.explanation: It disappears from emitted JavaScript.

title: Type Erasure and Runtime Reality
description: Understanding what TypeScript removes during compilation and what still exists in JavaScript.

blocks.content: Most TypeScript type syntax exists only during development and is erased before JavaScript runs. Interfaces, type aliases, generic parameters, and most annotations do not exist at runtime. This explains why `instanceof SomeInterface` is impossible and why API data still needs runtime validation.
keyPoints: Interfaces and type aliases are compile-time only.
Classes are runtime JavaScript values as well as TypeScript types.
Types cannot validate network responses by themselves.
Assertions affect the compiler, not runtime objects.

blocks.question: Why can't you write `if (value instanceof UserInterface)` when `UserInterface` is an interface?
blocks.answer: Because the interface does not exist in the emitted JavaScript. `instanceof` needs a real runtime constructor value.
blocks.explanation: Use a class, discriminant property, or runtime type guard depending on the data model.

blocks.question: A teammate says, 'The API response is safe because we defined an interface for it.' What is missing?
blocks.answer: The interface only checks code that already trusts that shape. It does not inspect the server response at runtime; external data should be validated when correctness matters.
blocks.explanation: Compile-time models and runtime validation solve different problems.

title: Declaration Merging
description: How compatible declarations with the same name can combine in TypeScript.

blocks.content: Certain TypeScript declarations with the same name can merge into one declaration. Interfaces are the most common example: declaring the same interface name multiple times combines its members. This is useful for library augmentation and ambient declarations, but accidental merging can also make large global type spaces harder to reason about.
keyPoints: Interfaces can merge; type aliases cannot be reopened.
Declaration merging is one reason interfaces are useful for extensible library contracts.
Prefer module-scoped augmentation over uncontrolled global declarations.

blocks.explanation: Both interface declarations contribute members to the final `AppConfig` type.

blocks.question: Can two `type User = ...` aliases with the same name merge like interfaces?
blocks.answer: No. Redeclaring the same type alias in the same scope is an error. Declaration merging is a capability of certain declarations such as interfaces, not type aliases.
blocks.explanation: This is a key practical difference between interface and type.

title: Avoiding any and Designing Safe Escape Hatches
description: Recognizing how any spreads and choosing safer alternatives.

blocks.content: `any` is an escape hatch that disables normal checking for the value and allows unsound operations to spread through later expressions. Sometimes it is unavoidable when migrating legacy code or integrating poorly typed libraries, but it should be contained at a narrow boundary and replaced with a safer type as soon as possible.
keyPoints: Prefer `unknown` when the value is uncertain but must be inspected safely.
Prefer a generic when the type is flexible but related to caller input/output.
Prefer a meaningful union or base interface when several known shapes are accepted.
If `any` is temporarily required, isolate it and document the boundary.

blocks.question: A shared utility is typed `function transform(data: any): any`. How would you decide what to replace it with?
blocks.answer: First identify the real relationship. If output matches input, use a generic. If input is untrusted, start with `unknown` and narrow. If only a finite set of shapes is valid, model a union or interface hierarchy.
blocks.explanation: The best replacement depends on whether the uncertainty is intentional, generic, or simply undocumented.

blocks.question: Why is `any` sometimes described as contagious?
blocks.answer: Operations performed on an any-typed value are unchecked and often produce more any-typed values, allowing type safety to disappear across a larger portion of the program.
blocks.explanation: One poorly typed boundary can weaken many otherwise well-typed consumers.
